description: Sentinel Engine offline threat intelligence database. Bundled for air-gapped deployments.

entries.title: Classic Single-Function Reentrancy
entries.description: A contract calls an external address before updating its own state, allowing the callee to re-enter the same function and drain funds. The canonical example is a withdraw function that sends ETH prior to zeroing the user's balance. Mitigation: apply the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern and/or use a reentrancy guard (e.g., OpenZeppelin ReentrancyGuard).
affected_patterns: external call before state update
call.value() before balance = 0
transfer before state change

entries.title: Cross-Function Reentrancy
entries.description: An attacker re-enters a different function in the same contract during an external call, exploiting shared mutable state that has not yet been updated. For instance, a withdraw function partially updates state while a transfer function reads the outdated value. Applying contract-wide reentrancy locks and using the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern across all functions mitigates the risk.
affected_patterns: shared state across multiple functions
partial state update before external call
cross-function shared balance variable

entries.title: Cross-Contract Reentrancy
entries.description: An attacker exploits reentrancy across multiple contracts that share state or trust relationships. Contract A calls Contract B which calls back into Contract C (or A again via a proxy), allowing stale state in any of the contracts to be abused. Comprehensive reentrancy guards on every entry point and minimal trust assumptions between contracts are required.
affected_patterns: inter-contract callbacks
mutual contract references
callback into trusted contract during external call

entries.title: Read-Only Reentrancy (View Function Manipulation)
entries.description: During a contract's execution (e.g., inside a receive/fallback hook), an attacker calls a view function on another protocol that reads transient/inconsistent state, then uses the manipulated read to influence a separate state-changing transaction. This bypasses classic reentrancy guards because the re-entered function is non-state-changing. Protocols that rely on external view calls for pricing or collateral checks are particularly vulnerable.
affected_patterns: view function reading price during callback
cross-protocol collateral check in callback
oracle read inside receive()

entries.title: ERC-777 Callback Reentrancy
entries.description: ERC-777 tokens invoke tokensToSend and tokensReceived hooks on sender/recipient contracts. An attacker deploying a malicious hook can re-enter the vulnerable contract before balances are settled, similar to the imBTC/Uniswap V1 exploit of April 2020. Projects integrating ERC-777 tokens must treat all token transfers as potentially reentrant and apply appropriate guards.
affected_patterns: ERC777 tokensReceived hook
ERC777 tokensToSend hook
IERC1820Registry hook callback

entries.title: Create2 Reentrancy / Deployment-Time Reentrancy
entries.description: During contract creation via CREATE2, the constructor body runs before the deployed address is registered as a contract. An attacker can deploy a contract whose constructor re-enters the deployer or factory, exploiting assumptions that the new address is not yet active. Factories that grant permissions or transfer assets upon CREATE2 deployment must validate that deployment is fully complete before granting access.
affected_patterns: CREATE2 deployment callback
factory granting permission in constructor
isContract() check bypass during construction

entries.title: Delegatecall Reentrancy
entries.description: A contract that uses delegatecall to an external library or logic contract can be re-entered if the callee itself makes external calls back to the caller's storage context. Because delegatecall shares storage, re-entering during a delegatecall execution can lead to unexpected state mutations. Logic contracts must be audited for their own external calls and reentrancy exposure.
affected_patterns: delegatecall to library with external calls
proxy delegatecall re-enter
logic contract calling external addresses

entries.title: Batch/Loop Reentrancy
entries.description: Functions that process multiple recipients or operations in a loop may re-enter on any iteration, allowing an attacker to manipulate loop counters or shared state mid-execution. The vulnerability is particularly acute in airdrop, multi-send, and batch-liquidation functions. Ensure reentrancy guards cover the entire batch function and state updates precede external calls in each iteration.
affected_patterns: for loop with external call
multi-recipient transfer loop
batch liquidation with callbacks

entries.title: Flash Loan Price Manipulation
entries.description: An attacker borrows a large amount of tokens via flash loan and uses them to heavily manipulate the spot price on a low-liquidity AMM that the target protocol reads as an oracle. The manipulated price is then exploited (e.g., over-borrowing, artificially high collateral valuation) before the flash loan is repaid within a single transaction. Protocols must use time-weighted average prices (TWAP) or Chainlink feeds instead of spot prices for critical calculations.
affected_patterns: spot price oracle
AMM reserve-based price calculation
getReserves() used as price source

entries.title: Flash Loan Governance Attack
entries.description: An attacker flash-borrows a large number of governance tokens, votes to pass a malicious proposal (or exercises a snapshot-based voting mechanism), then repays the loan — all within a single block. Governance systems that use current token balance as voting power without a time-lock or delegation snapshot are vulnerable. Mitigations include requiring vote-weight snapshots from a previous block and enforcing multi-day time-locks on proposal execution.
affected_patterns: token balance as voting power
same-block vote and repay
governance without snapshot

entries.title: Flash Loan Liquidation Exploit
entries.description: An attacker uses a flash loan to temporarily push a borrower's collateral ratio below the liquidation threshold (by dumping collateral price on an AMM oracle), executes the liquidation for a profit, and repays the flash loan. The profit comes from the liquidation bonus being larger than the price impact cost. Protocols must ensure that liquidation calculations use manipulation-resistant prices and that liquidation bonuses do not create risk-free arbitrage.
affected_patterns: liquidation based on manipulable oracle
AMM-sourced collateral price
liquidation bonus exceeding price impact

entries.title: Flash Mint Abuse
entries.description: Protocols that allow minting unbounded token supply within a single transaction (flash mint) can be abused to artificially inflate total supply, break invariants relying on supply calculations, or manipulate systems that use total supply as a denominator. EIP-3156 compliant flash minters should enforce hard caps and ensure that all protocol invariants hold under maximum supply conditions.
affected_patterns: unbounded flash mint
totalSupply() as price denominator
ERC20 flashMint without cap

entries.title: Flash Loan Sandwich / Atomic Arbitrage
entries.description: An attacker uses a flash loan to perform a sandwich attack atomically: buy a token, trigger the victim's transaction which inflates the price further, then sell — all in one transaction without needing upfront capital. This removes the capital requirement from classic sandwich attacks and increases their feasibility. Protocols can defend by adding deadlines, slippage checks, and private mempools (e.g., Flashbots Protect).
affected_patterns: large single-tx buy/sell around victim tx
AMM without slippage protection
atomicSandwich

entries.title: Spot Price Manipulation via AMM
entries.description: When a DeFi protocol reads token prices directly from AMM reserves (e.g., Uniswap V2 getReserves()) rather than a TWAP or Chainlink feed, a well-funded attacker can manipulate the price within a single block to exploit lending, derivatives, or liquidation logic. Even without a flash loan, a large trade followed by protocol interaction and a rebalancing trade can be atomic and profitable. Use multi-block TWAP oracles or Chainlink for all pricing.
affected_patterns: getReserves() price calculation
reserve0/reserve1 spot price
UniswapV2 price oracle

entries.title: TWAP Manipulation (Multi-Block)
entries.description: While TWAP oracles are resistant to single-block manipulation, an attacker with sustained block production influence (e.g., a validator or block builder colluding over multiple blocks) can gradually skew a short TWAP window. Very short TWAP periods (e.g., 1-2 minutes) on low-liquidity pools are especially susceptible. Protocols should use TWAP windows of at least 30 minutes and monitor for oracle anomalies.
affected_patterns: short TWAP window (< 30 min)
low-liquidity TWAP pool
Uniswap V3 observe() with short period

entries.title: Chainlink Stale Price Feed
entries.description: Chainlink oracles do not update on every block; a heartbeat interval (typically 1 hour) governs updates. If a protocol does not check the updatedAt timestamp and compare it against an acceptable staleness threshold, stale prices can be used during high-volatility periods or after a Chainlink oracle outage. Always validate latestRoundData() results: check that answeredInRound >= roundId and that updatedAt is within an acceptable window.
affected_patterns: latestAnswer() without staleness check
latestRoundData() without timestamp validation
AggregatorV3Interface without answeredInRound check

entries.title: Oracle Frontrunning
entries.description: When an on-chain oracle update is visible in the mempool before inclusion, an attacker can frontrun the update transaction to interact with the protocol at the old (stale) price and then benefit from the new price. This is common in perpetuals and options protocols that use push-based oracles. Using commit-reveal schemes, private mempools, or pull-based oracle architectures (e.g., Pyth, Stork) mitigates this risk.
affected_patterns: push oracle update frontrun
oracle price update in mempool
position opening before oracle update

entries.title: Uniswap V2 Reserve Manipulation
entries.description: Direct ERC-20 token transfers to a Uniswap V2 pair contract (bypassing the router) artificially inflate one reserve without minting LP tokens, skewing the reserve ratio used by getReserves(). Any protocol that computes prices from raw reserve values without relying on the official router is vulnerable to this low-cost manipulation. Always use Uniswap's cumulative price accumulators or an independent oracle.
affected_patterns: direct ERC20 transfer to pair contract
getReserves() without sync()
token donation to LP pair

entries.title: tx.origin Authentication Bypass
entries.description: Using tx.origin for authentication checks identifies the original EOA that started the transaction chain, not the immediate caller (msg.sender). An attacker can trick a legitimate EOA into sending a transaction through a malicious contract, which then calls the vulnerable contract — tx.origin matches the victim EOA while msg.sender is the attacker's contract. Replace all tx.origin authentication with msg.sender checks.
affected_patterns: require(tx.origin == owner)
tx.origin authorization
tx.origin != msg.sender check bypassed

entries.title: Missing Access Control on Critical Functions
entries.description: Administrative or privileged functions (e.g., mint, pause, upgrade, setOracle) lack an onlyOwner or role-based guard, allowing any address to invoke them. This is a direct path to complete protocol compromise. Every state-changing function that affects protocol-wide parameters must be protected by an explicit access control modifier and audited for completeness.
affected_patterns: public mint without restriction
unprotected setOwner()
unguarded pause/unpause
missing onlyOwner modifier

entries.title: Unprotected initialize() in Proxies
entries.description: Upgradeable proxy contracts that use an initialize() function instead of a constructor can be front-run: if the proxy deployer does not call initialize() atomically in the same transaction, an attacker can call it first and become the owner or set malicious parameters. The implementation contract's initialize() function is also callable directly if the implementation is not self-destructed or locked. Use OpenZeppelin's initializer modifier and call initialize() in the deployment transaction.
affected_patterns: initialize() without initializer modifier
proxy deployment without immediate initialization
implementation contract directly initializable

entries.title: Default Visibility (pre-Solidity 0.5.0)
entries.description: In Solidity versions prior to 0.5.0, functions without an explicit visibility keyword default to public, unintentionally exposing sensitive internal logic. An attacker can call these functions to manipulate state, drain funds, or bypass business logic. All contracts should explicitly specify visibility modifiers, and audits of legacy codebases should flag missing modifiers as critical findings.
affected_patterns: function without visibility specifier
implicit public function
solidity <0.5.0 default visibility

entries.title: Centralization Risk (Single Admin Key)
entries.description: A single EOA holding owner or admin privileges represents a critical single point of failure: compromise of that private key allows complete protocol control including upgrading contracts, draining treasuries, and pausing operations. Mitigate by using multi-signature wallets (e.g., Gnosis Safe with 3-of-5 threshold), timelocks, and role separation. Governance functions with significant value impact should require on-chain governance votes.
affected_patterns: single owner EOA
Ownable without multisig
no timelock on admin actions

entries.title: Unprotected selfdestruct
entries.description: A selfdestruct opcode call without proper access controls allows any caller to destroy the contract and force-send its ETH balance to an arbitrary address. This is irreversible, permanently breaking the protocol. Libraries used via delegatecall are especially dangerous because a selfdestruct in the library context destroys the calling contract. Remove selfdestruct from non-emergency code and gate any emergency kill switch behind a multisig with a timelock.
affected_patterns: unprotected selfdestruct()
selfdestruct in delegatecall target
kill() function without access control

entries.title: Missing Two-Step Ownership Transfer
entries.description: Single-step ownership transfers (transferOwnership(newOwner)) immediately set the new owner without requiring acceptance. If a wrong address is provided (typo, zero address, or compromised address), ownership is irreversibly lost. OpenZeppelin's Ownable2Step requires the new owner to explicitly call acceptOwnership(), providing a safeguard against accidental transfers. All ownership transfers in high-value contracts should use the two-step pattern.
affected_patterns: transferOwnership() single step
owner = newOwner without acceptance
Ownable without Ownable2Step

entries.title: Unprotected Function in Role-Based Access System
entries.description: Role-based access control (e.g., AccessControl) is implemented, but one or more critical functions miss a role check due to copy-paste errors or oversight during development. Systematic role matrix audits—mapping every function to its required role—should be performed. Automated tools should verify that all state-changing functions have an explicit access control annotation.
affected_patterns: AccessControl with missing hasRole check
function bypassing role guard
onlyRole modifier absent on state-change function

entries.title: Integer Overflow (pre-Solidity 0.8.0)
entries.description: In Solidity versions prior to 0.8.0, arithmetic operations on unsigned integers silently wrap on overflow (e.g., uint8(255) + 1 == 0). Attackers can exploit this to bypass balance checks, mint unlimited tokens, or underflow withdrawal balances. The BatchOverflow exploit (BEC token, 2018) allowed minting 2^256 tokens via a multiplication overflow. Use SafeMath for all arithmetic in pre-0.8.0 code or upgrade to Solidity >=0.8.0.
affected_patterns: uint arithmetic without SafeMath (<0.8.0)
unchecked multiplication
balance += amount without overflow check

entries.title: Integer Underflow (pre-Solidity 0.8.0)
entries.description: Unsigned integer subtraction that goes below zero silently wraps to a very large number in Solidity < 0.8.0. An attacker who passes a withdrawal amount larger than their balance can end up with a near-maximal uint256 balance. Always use SafeMath.sub() in legacy code and validate that sufficient balance exists before subtraction.
affected_patterns: uint balance -= withdrawal without check (<0.8.0)
require(balance >= amount) missing
sub without SafeMath

entries.title: Unsafe Type Casting (uint256 to smaller uint)
entries.description: Explicit downcasting (e.g., uint128(largeValue)) silently truncates bits, potentially reducing a large value to a near-zero or zero result without reverting. In Solidity 0.8.x, this still does not revert; only SafeCast (OpenZeppelin) will revert on overflow. Downcasting is especially dangerous in fee calculations, token amounts, and timestamp comparisons. Use SafeCast.toUint128() for all downcasting operations.
affected_patterns: uint128(value) without bounds check
explicit narrowing cast
int256 to int128 truncation

entries.title: Division Before Multiplication (Precision Loss)
entries.description: Integer division in Solidity truncates towards zero; performing division before multiplication magnifies precision loss. For example, (a / b) * c loses far more precision than (a * c) / b when b does not evenly divide a. This is common in fee and interest rate calculations, where small errors accumulate over time or can be gamed. Always perform multiplications before divisions and use sufficient fixed-point scaling (e.g., 1e18 basis).
affected_patterns: (a / b) * c pattern
fee calculation with early division
ratio computation before scaling

entries.title: Rounding Errors in Token Calculations
entries.description: Token share/amount conversions (e.g., shares-to-assets in ERC-4626 vaults) can accumulate rounding errors that favor attackers or disadvantage users over many transactions. An attacker can systematically extract value by repeatedly calling functions that round in their favor. Protocols should round in the direction that is unfavorable to the caller (down for minting, up for redeeming) and use virtual shares to mitigate first-depositor inflation attacks.
affected_patterns: shares * totalAssets / totalSupply without rounding direction
ERC4626 convertToShares rounding
repeated small-amount rounding profit

entries.title: Signature Replay (Missing Nonce)
entries.description: Off-chain signatures that lack a nonce or unique transaction identifier can be replayed by anyone who captures a valid signature. For example, a user's signature authorizing a token transfer can be submitted multiple times, draining their balance. All signed messages must include a nonce (incremented after use), chain ID, and contract address to prevent replay attacks across transactions and networks. Use EIP-712 structured data signing.
affected_patterns: ecrecover without nonce validation
signed message reuse
missing nonces mapping
EIP-712 without chainId

entries.title: Signature Malleability (ECDSA s-value)
entries.description: ECDSA signatures have two valid representations for the same signing operation (due to the curve's symmetry): one with s in the lower half-order and one in the upper half-order. Using the raw ecrecover precompile without enforcing s <= secp256k1n/2 allows an adversary to produce a second valid signature from a first, potentially bypassing replay protection based on signature hash uniqueness. Always use OpenZeppelin's ECDSA.recover() which enforces the lower-s constraint.
affected_patterns: raw ecrecover() call
signature uniqueness without s-value check
ECDSA without malleability guard

entries.title: Missing Deadline on EIP-2612 Permits
entries.description: EIP-2612 permit() allows gasless token approvals via off-chain signatures. If the signed message omits a deadline or the contract does not enforce deadline <= block.timestamp, permits remain valid indefinitely. An attacker who captures an old permit signature can execute it at any future time, potentially granting themselves token allowances that the user intended to be temporary. Always include and enforce deadlines in permit signatures.
affected_patterns: permit() without deadline enforcement
EIP2612 with deadline = type(uint256).max
allowance signature without expiry

entries.title: ecrecover Returns address(0) Without Check
entries.description: The ecrecover precompile returns address(0) for invalid or malformed signatures rather than reverting. If the result is not checked against address(0) and compared to an expected signer, an attacker can pass an invalid signature and impersonate any address that is also (incorrectly) using address(0) as an admin or signer. Always require(signer != address(0)) after ecrecover and verify against the expected authorized address.
affected_patterns: ecrecover return value not checked for zero
require(signer == expected) missing zero check
address(0) admin bypass via invalid signature

entries.title: Cross-Chain Signature Replay
entries.description: Signatures valid on one EVM-compatible chain can be replayed on another chain if the signed message does not include the chain ID. After hard forks or multi-chain deployments of the same contract bytecode, users' signatures may be replayable across chains. EIP-155 (for transactions) and EIP-712 (for typed data) both include the chain ID; custom signature schemes must do the same.
affected_patterns: signed message without chainId
signature valid across chains
same contract address on multiple chains

entries.title: Storage Collision in Proxy Patterns
entries.description: In transparent or UUPS proxy patterns, the proxy and implementation contract share the same storage layout. If the implementation contract's variable ordering is changed during an upgrade, or if the proxy's admin storage slot collides with the implementation's slot 0, critical variables can be overwritten. EIP-1967 defines dedicated storage slots for proxy metadata to avoid collisions. Always use EIP-1967-compliant proxy patterns and verify storage layouts between upgrades using tools like slither-check-upgradeability.
affected_patterns: proxy and implementation storage overlap
slot 0 admin variable collision
non-EIP1967 proxy storage

entries.title: Uninitialized Proxy Implementation
entries.description: The implementation contract (logic contract) behind a proxy can be directly called and its initialize() function invoked by an attacker if the implementation is deployed without being initialized. This is separate from the proxy state: the implementation's own storage can be initialized to set malicious values, which in some patterns can affect the proxy or be used to call selfdestruct on the implementation, permanently bricking the proxy. Always initialize the implementation contract immediately upon deployment.
affected_patterns: implementation contract not initialized
logic contract accessible directly
implementation selfdestruct via direct call

entries.title: Function Selector Clashing
entries.description: Solidity function selectors are the first 4 bytes of the keccak256 hash of the function signature. Two different function signatures can share the same 4-byte selector (collision). In proxy patterns and Diamond (EIP-2535) implementations, a selector clash between proxy and implementation can cause admin functions to be silently hijacked or logic functions to call the wrong target. Selector clash audits are mandatory for all proxy deployments.
affected_patterns: 4-byte selector collision
Diamond proxy selector clash
proxy admin function hidden by implementation

entries.title: UUPS Missing Upgrade Authorization
entries.description: In the UUPS (Universal Upgradeable Proxy Standard) pattern, the upgrade logic resides in the implementation contract. If _authorizeUpgrade() is not properly overridden with access control, any user can trigger an upgrade to a malicious implementation, taking full control of the proxy. OpenZeppelin's UUPSUpgradeable requires _authorizeUpgrade() to be overridden; forgetting to add onlyOwner (or equivalent) is a known audit finding. Always test that unauthorized callers cannot trigger upgrades.
affected_patterns: _authorizeUpgrade() without access control
UUPS upgradeTo() callable by anyone
UUPSUpgradeable missing override

entries.title: Delegatecall to Untrusted Contract
entries.description: delegatecall executes the callee's bytecode in the caller's storage context, allowing the callee to read and overwrite any storage slot including owner, balances, and access control mappings. If the target of a delegatecall is user-controlled or set to an untrusted address, the caller contract is fully compromised. The Parity wallet hack (2017) exploited this: a delegatecall to a library whose initWallet() was not protected allowed an attacker to seize ownership of every multi-sig wallet.
affected_patterns: delegatecall to user-supplied address
delegatecall to mutable library address
low-level delegatecall without whitelist

entries.title: AMM Rounding Errors in Uniswap V2 Forks
entries.description: Uniswap V2's constant-product formula uses integer arithmetic and rounds down by default. Forks that modify fee structures or liquidity formulas without careful rounding analysis introduce systematic precision loss that can be exploited via repeated small transactions. Over time, attackers can drain residual amounts or cause invariant k to decrease, destabilizing pool prices. All AMM forks must be independently verified for arithmetic correctness.
affected_patterns: x * y = k rounding deviation
liquidity calculation floor division
getAmountOut precision loss

entries.title: Compound Oracle Staleness in Forks
entries.description: Compound V2 forks that use a copy of the price oracle without updating to live feeds may continue reading prices from an outdated or abandoned oracle contract after deployment. Stale collateral prices can enable over-borrowing or prevent legitimate liquidations. All forked protocols must audit their oracle dependencies and establish freshness checks with fallback mechanisms.
affected_patterns: Compound fork with unchanged oracle address
price oracle returning stale last value
PriceOracle not updated post-fork

entries.title: Missing Slippage Protection
entries.description: DEX integrations and liquidity provision functions that accept amountOutMin = 0 (or equivalent) expose users to unlimited slippage from sandwich attacks and pool imbalances. A transaction that completes at an arbitrarily unfavorable price is accepted without reversion. All AMM interactions must enforce a user-specified (or protocol-enforced) minimum output and revert if slippage exceeds the threshold.
affected_patterns: amountOutMin = 0
swapExactTokensForTokens without slippage
addLiquidity without price bounds

entries.title: Fee-on-Transfer Token Accounting
entries.description: Some ERC-20 tokens deduct a fee on every transfer, so the amount received is less than the amount sent. Protocols that credit the sent amount (rather than the actually received amount) maintain incorrect internal accounting, leading to insolvency over time and enabling attackers to withdraw more than they deposited. Always measure balances before and after transfers (balance delta pattern) rather than trusting the transfer amount parameter.
affected_patterns: transfer amount credited without balance check
safeTransferFrom amount assumed received in full
deflationary token deposit accounting

entries.title: Sandwich Attack Surface (No Deadline on AMM Calls)
entries.description: Swap transactions submitted without a deadline parameter (or with deadline = type(uint256).max) can sit in the mempool indefinitely and be executed at an arbitrary future time when market conditions favor a sandwich attacker. Adding a deadline ensures that stale transactions expire and cannot be exploited by miners or MEV bots. All user-facing AMM integrations must require a deadline no further than a few minutes in the future.
affected_patterns: deadline = type(uint256).max
swapExactTokensForTokens with far-future deadline
AMM interaction without deadline

entries.title: First Depositor Share Inflation Attack
entries.description: In ERC-4626 or yield-bearing vaults with zero initial supply, the first depositor can deposit 1 wei, then directly donate a large amount to the vault to inflate the share price. Subsequent depositors receive 0 shares due to rounding (their deposit amount < share price), effectively losing their entire deposit to the first depositor. The mitigation is to use virtual shares (offset) or ensure a minimum deposit amount that makes the attack unprofitable.
affected_patterns: ERC4626 first depositor rounding
totalSupply = 0 share minting
vault share inflation via donation

entries.title: Donation Attack on Vault Shares
entries.description: An attacker directly transfers tokens (donates) to a vault contract's balance, inflating the assets-per-share ratio beyond what existing share minting accounts for. This can grief legitimate depositors by making their deposits receive fewer shares and their withdrawals receive less value. Vaults should track deposited amounts independently of raw token balances or use virtual shares to neutralize direct donation attacks.
affected_patterns: totalAssets() relying on balanceOf(address(this))
direct ERC20 transfer to vault
share price manipulation via donation

entries.title: Rebasing Token Integration Errors
entries.description: Rebasing tokens (e.g., AMPL, stETH) adjust user balances automatically via elastic supply mechanics. Protocols that cache or snapshot balances without accounting for rebases maintain incorrect state, allowing users to withdraw more (positive rebase) or less (negative rebase) than their fair share. All DeFi protocols integrating rebasing tokens must use wrapper tokens (wstETH) or dynamically compute balances at every interaction.
affected_patterns: cached balance with rebasing token
stETH balance snapshot
AMPL integration without rebase accounting

entries.title: Flash Loan Voting Attack
entries.description: An attacker uses a flash loan to borrow a large quantity of governance tokens, cast decisive votes on a malicious proposal (or cancel a beneficial one), and repay the loan — all within a single transaction or block. Governance systems without delegation-based snapshots or lock periods are fully vulnerable. The Beanstalk attack (April 2022) used a $1B flash loan to pass a governance proposal that drained the protocol's $182M treasury.
affected_patterns: governance token balance as voting power at current block
proposal creation and voting in same tx
no token lock period for voting

entries.title: Proposal Frontrunning in Governance
entries.description: When governance proposals are submitted as plain-text transactions in the mempool, sophisticated actors can observe the proposal content, frontrun it by creating a competing or canceling proposal, or rapidly accumulate voting power to influence the vote outcome before others can react. Using commit-reveal proposal submission schemes or private mempools for proposal creation mitigates this risk.
affected_patterns: proposal content visible in mempool
proposal frontrun before quorum
governance proposal cancellation frontrun

entries.title: Vote Buying via Token Lending
entries.description: Governance tokens can be borrowed from lending protocols (e.g., Aave, Compound) for the duration of a vote, used to pass a malicious proposal, and returned after the vote concludes. Unlike flash loan attacks, this approach works even in governance systems with block-based snapshots, as the tokens are held across blocks. Protocols should consider non-transferable voting representations, vote-escrow mechanisms (veTokens), or mandatory cooldown periods.
affected_patterns: borrowed governance token voting
temporary token accumulation for vote
delegated borrowed token governance

entries.title: Governance Time-Lock Bypass
entries.description: Time-locks are a critical safeguard allowing the community to detect and react to malicious governance proposals before execution. Protocols that implement a TimelockController may have emergency bypass functions (guardian, cancel authority) that can themselves be exploited or misused. Additionally, if the time-lock delay is set too short (e.g., 2 hours), users have insufficient time to exit before a harmful upgrade executes. Minimum delays of 48-72 hours are recommended for high-value protocols.
affected_patterns: TimelockController with short delay
guardian can bypass timelock
emergency execute without delay

entries.title: Sandwich Attack on Swaps
entries.description: MEV searchers monitor the mempool for large pending swap transactions and wrap them with a frontrun (buy before the victim's transaction increases price) and a backrun (sell after the victim's transaction), profiting from the price impact caused by the victim. The victim receives fewer tokens than expected, with the difference being extracted by the sandwich bot. Users should set tight slippage tolerances, use private mempools, or use MEV-protected RPC endpoints.
affected_patterns: large AMM swap with loose slippage
no deadline on swap
public mempool swap transaction

entries.title: Liquidation Frontrunning
entries.description: When an undercollateralized position is submitted for liquidation, MEV bots in the mempool can detect the transaction and frontrun it with their own liquidation call at a higher gas price, capturing the liquidation bonus. The original liquidator's transaction either fails (position already liquidated) or loses the profit. While this is a competitive dynamic rather than a security flaw, protocols can implement a fair-launch liquidation queue or partial liquidation mechanics to mitigate bot dominance.
affected_patterns: public liquidate() call in mempool
liquidation bonus captured by frontrunner
liquidation without priority ordering

entries.title: Transaction Ordering Dependence (TOD)
entries.description: Contract logic that produces different outcomes depending on transaction ordering within a block can be exploited by validators or MEV bots who control block composition. Examples include race conditions on first-come-first-served token claims, price-dependent trade execution, and contest winner selection. Protocols must assume that transaction ordering can be arbitrary and design mechanisms that are ordering-agnostic, or use commit-reveal schemes.
affected_patterns: first-come-first-served token claim
ordering-sensitive state machine
race condition on limited resource

entries.title: Backrunning Arbitrage Exposure
entries.description: Any transaction that moves an on-chain price away from fair market value creates a backrunning opportunity for arbitrageurs. While backrunning arbitrage stabilizes prices, excessive arbitrage leakage represents a cost paid by protocol users (liquidity providers, traders). Protocols can reduce this leakage through dynamic fee adjustments, just-in-time liquidity mechanisms, or integrating with MEV-aware infrastructure that returns arbitrage profit to LPs.
affected_patterns: large trade creating arbitrage opportunity
oracle update creating backrun
LP price deviation from CEX

entries.title: Unchecked Return Value of External Call
entries.description: Low-level calls (call, delegatecall, send) return a boolean indicating success or failure; they do not revert on failure. Ignoring the return value means silent failures can leave the contract in an inconsistent state (e.g., believing a transfer succeeded when it did not). The King of the Ether Throne contract lost ETH because of unchecked send() failures. Always use SafeERC20 for token transfers and check return values of all low-level calls.
affected_patterns: unchecked call() return value
.send() without success check
low-level call result ignored

entries.title: Denial of Service via Unexpected Revert
entries.description: If a contract iterates over a list of recipients and calls external addresses (e.g., to distribute ETH), a single recipient that always reverts can permanently block the entire distribution loop. This is a denial-of-service vulnerability allowing a malicious participant to freeze protocol operations. The pattern is common in voting dividend contracts and airdrop mechanisms. Use the withdrawal pattern (pull over push) to let each recipient claim individually.
affected_patterns: push payment to multiple recipients
loop with external call that may revert
ETH distribution to contract addresses

entries.title: Weak Randomness (block.timestamp / blockhash)
entries.description: Using block.timestamp or blockhash as a source of randomness is insecure because miners/validators can influence these values to bias outcomes in their favor. This is especially critical for on-chain lotteries, NFT trait generation, and randomized reward distribution. Use Chainlink VRF or commit-reveal schemes for verifiable on-chain randomness that cannot be manipulated by block producers.
affected_patterns: block.timestamp % N as random
blockhash(block.number - 1) as seed
block.difficulty for randomness (pre-PoS)

entries.title: Improper Input Validation on Token Amounts
entries.description: Functions that accept user-provided token amounts without validating bounds (e.g., zero amounts, amounts exceeding supply, or amounts causing invariant violations) can lead to division-by-zero errors, zero-value events that confuse off-chain indexers, or unexpected behavior in downstream calculations. All token amount parameters should be validated to be within acceptable ranges before processing.
affected_patterns: deposit(0) without revert
withdraw amount exceeding balance not checked
zero amount transfer allowed

entries.title: Timestamp Manipulation (block.timestamp Dependence)
entries.description: Validators can manipulate block.timestamp within a small range (typically ±15 seconds) to influence time-sensitive contract logic such as lock expiry, interest accrual, and epoch boundaries. Contracts that use block.timestamp for fine-grained time calculations are vulnerable to subtle manipulation that could allow early unlocking or skewed reward accrual. Use block.number for relative timing where possible and avoid sub-minute precision requirements.
affected_patterns: block.timestamp for lock expiry
time-based reward calculation
block.timestamp compared to user input

entries.title: Incorrect Event Emission / Silent State Mutation
entries.description: Contracts that modify critical state (ownership changes, parameter updates, large transfers) without emitting corresponding events leave off-chain monitoring systems blind to important protocol changes. Silent state mutations can allow attackers to operate undetected during an exploit and make post-hoc forensic analysis extremely difficult. All state-changing operations of significance must emit descriptive events with indexed fields for efficient off-chain querying.
affected_patterns: ownership transfer without event
parameter change without emit
missing Transfer/Approval events

entries.title: Uniswap V4 Hook Re-entrancy During Swap/Liquidity Operations
entries.description: Uniswap V4 hooks execute user-defined code during swap and liquidity operations via beforeSwap() and afterSwap() callbacks. A malicious hook can re-enter the pool contract during execution, manipulating reserves, balances, or hook state mid-operation. Unlike V3, hooks have full access to pool internals. Because hooks are directly called by the pool and execute arbitrary code, improper reentrancy guards in hook implementations allow attackers to drain liquidity pools, manipulate prices, or steal fees. The vulnerability is amplified in V4 because hooks can trigger multiple callback types (mint, burn, swap, donate) creating complex re-entry chains.
affected_patterns: beforeSwap() hook without ReentrancyGuard or mutex
afterSwap() hook making external calls
hook calling pool.swap() recursively
cross-hook reentrancy (mint hook calling swap hook)
beforeSwap() reading pool state without accounting for in-progress operations
hook contract inheriting from IHooks without reentrancy protection
flashSwap callback into hook context without guards

entries.title: Malicious Fee-on-Transfer Hook Silently Drains Tokens
entries.description: A hook contract implementing beforeSwap() or afterSwap() callbacks can embed hidden fee logic that siphons tokens during token transfers. By implementing custom hook logic that reads token amounts and silently transfers a percentage to an attacker-controlled address during swap execution, the hook can drain value without being obvious in the swap event logs. This is particularly dangerous in wrapped token scenarios where the hook contract mediates token transfers. Attackers can disguise the fee as a legitimate protocol fee or flash loan repayment premium, bypassing user slippage checks because the fee is extracted at hook execution time, after the swap has been executed.
affected_patterns: beforeSwap() hook transferring tokens to external address
afterSwap() hook with unchecked external token transfers
hook calling token.transfer() without event emission
beforeSwap() subtracting from amount0/amount1 before returning
hook receiving tokens and not returning them
multiple hooks on same pool with chain of transfers
hook with delegatecall to proxy contract controlling token flow

entries.title: Flash Loan Callback Manipulation Through Hook State Injection
entries.description: During a pool's flash loan callback (or beforeSwap hook), an attacker can trigger the execution of hook code that manipulates the state read by downstream operations. In Uniswap V4, hooks have access to PoolKey, balances, liquidity, and fee data. An attacker can craft a sequence where: (1) a flash loan is initiated, (2) the beforeSwap hook fires and modifies hook state or calls back into the pool, (3) the callback sees stale/manipulated state and makes incorrect decisions about pricing or collateral. The attack exploits the fact that hooks run synchronously during pool operations and can influence the execution context of subsequently-called hooks or external contracts that depend on pool invariants.
affected_patterns: beforeSwap() hook modifying hook storage during flash operation
afterSwap() hook reading state modified by beforeSwap() without validation
hook callback during flash loan re-entering with delegatecall
hook using tx.origin or msg.sender to identify caller, vulnerable to sandwich
hook state not reset on reentry, causing state leakage across callbacks
hook calling balanceOf() or getReserves() during callback execution
hook without proper flash accounting sync (not calling settleBalance)

entries.title: PoolManager Access Control Bypass in Hook Functions
entries.description: Uniswap V4 hook callback functions (beforeSwap, afterSwap, beforeAddLiquidity, afterAddLiquidity, beforeRemoveLiquidity, afterRemoveLiquidity, beforeDonate, afterDonate) must restrict callers exclusively to the official PoolManager contract. Developers frequently omit this access control check, allowing attackers to invoke hook callbacks directly without executing a real swap or liquidity operation. By calling hook functions directly, an attacker can manipulate the hook's internal state — updating accumulators, claiming rewards, modifying fee parameters, or corrupting bookkeeping variables — without any corresponding pool-level token movement. This is especially dangerous when hooks maintain accounting state (e.g., cumulative fees, LP reward points, or governance votes) that downstream contracts rely on for correctness.
affected_patterns: hook callback function missing msg.sender == poolManager check
beforeSwap() or afterSwap() callable by any external address
hook using onlyOwner instead of onlyPoolManager modifier
hook with public/external callback functions lacking caller validation
hook inheriting BaseHook but overriding without calling super access check
hook accepting arbitrary PoolKey parameter without verifying pool registration
hook functions missing require(msg.sender == address(poolManager)) guard

entries.title: Flash Accounting Delta Settlement Failure via Malicious Hook
entries.description: Uniswap V4's singleton PoolManager architecture uses EIP-1153 transient storage for flash accounting, requiring all token deltas to settle to zero by the end of each transaction. A malicious or buggy hook can manipulate these deltas during callback execution — claiming fees, minting liquidity credits, or modifying currency balances without properly burning the corresponding transient debt. If a hook increments its own balance delta (e.g., via take()) without a matching settle(), or if it manipulates the PoolManager's internal accounting through crafted return values, it can drain tokens from the pool while leaving the settlement check satisfied through offsetting manipulations across multiple currency pairs. This attack vector is unique to V4's singleton architecture where all pools share a single contract's transient storage.
affected_patterns: hook calling poolManager.take() without corresponding settle()
hook modifying BalanceDelta return values in beforeSwap/afterSwap
hook using transient storage (tstore/tload) to manipulate settlement state
afterSwap() hook claiming fees without burning transient debt
hook exploiting cross-pool delta netting in singleton PoolManager
hook returning manipulated toBeforeSwapDelta or toAfterSwapDelta values
hook calling mint() or donate() during callback without proper delta accounting

entries.title: Custom Oracle Manipulation via Hook State Update Ordering
entries.description: Hooks frequently serve as custom pricing oracles for external protocols — providing TWAP calculations, spot price feeds, or volatility metrics. When a hook updates its internal price state in beforeSwap() (before the swap executes) or in afterSwap() without time-weighted protections, a flash loan attacker can skew the price ratio within a single transaction and force the hook to record a manipulated price. The attack sequence is: (1) flash loan large token amount, (2) execute a swap that triggers the hook's price update, (3) use the now-corrupted oracle price in an external protocol (lending, options, liquidations), (4) reverse the swap and repay the flash loan. Without TWAP smoothing, minimum observation windows, slippage bounds, or multi-block price validation, the hook's oracle becomes a single-transaction manipulation vector that downstream DeFi protocols blindly trust.
affected_patterns: hook updating price oracle state in beforeSwap() before swap execution
afterSwap() hook recording spot price without TWAP or EMA smoothing
hook oracle lacking minimum time interval between price updates
hook exposing price feed without multi-block validation or delay
hook price update using instantaneous reserves instead of cumulative values
hook oracle readable by external contracts without staleness check
hook price state modifiable by single large swap without slippage circuit breaker

entries.title: Bridge Message Authenticity Verification Failure
entries.description: Bridge relay contracts that fail to properly verify the authenticity of cross-chain messages allow attackers to forge messages claiming token deposits on the source chain that never occurred, causing the destination bridge to mint or release unbacked tokens. The Nomad bridge hack ($190M) exploited exactly this flaw — a faulty message verification routine allowed any arbitrary message to be treated as proven without a valid Merkle proof. Root causes include missing Merkle proof validation against the committed state root, validator signature threshold checks that fall below Byzantine fault tolerance (requiring at least n/3+1 signatures), failure to mark message hashes as consumed after processing (enabling replay), accepting messages before source chain transaction finality is confirmed, and using tx.origin instead of msg.sender for message sender verification. Protocols relying on light clients or optimistic verification must implement the full proof verification pipeline without shortcuts.
affected_patterns: bridge accepting messages without Merkle proof verification against committed state root
validator signature threshold below Byzantine fault tolerance (fewer than n/3+1 validators required)
message hash not marked as consumed after processing — allows replay of same message
cross-chain message relay without source chain finality confirmation (e.g., accepting 1-block-old state)
bridge contract using tx.origin for message sender verification instead of msg.sender
missing nonce tracking per source-destination channel allowing message replay attacks

entries.title: Bridge Validator Key Compromise and Multisig Threshold Weakness
entries.description: Bridges secured by multisig schemes or external validator sets where the signing threshold is too low, or where validators share cloud infrastructure, are vulnerable to coordinated key compromise. The Ronin bridge hack ($625M) succeeded by compromising just 5 of 9 validators — four through a single spear-phishing campaign and one via a gas-free RPC backdoor. Risk factors include: a multisig threshold set below 2/3 of total signers (insufficient for Byzantine fault tolerance), validators co-located in the same cloud provider or data center (correlated failure), absence of a key rotation mechanism meaning a compromised key remains valid indefinitely, and validator set updates that can be applied immediately without a governance timelock. Bridges must enforce a high threshold (typically 2/3+1), mandate geographic and infrastructure diversity among validators, provide an emergency key rotation path, and require timelocked governance approval for validator set changes.
affected_patterns: multisig threshold below 2/3 of total signers (e.g., 5-of-9 threshold is insufficient)
validator set updatable by a single admin address without timelock delay
bridge using EOA-controlled validators instead of smart-contract-based validation with slashing
no mechanism for emergency validator key rotation after suspected compromise
validator signatures not verified against a registered and active validator set on-chain
bridge continuing to accept signatures from validators that have been formally removed

entries.title: Canonical vs Wrapped Token Confusion in Bridge Transfers
entries.description: Bridges that fail to properly distinguish between canonical (natively issued) tokens and their wrapped representations across chains create conditions for double-counting or unbacked minting. The attack pattern: an attacker deposits wrapped tokens on chain A; the bridge, lacking a rigorous token registry, incorrectly classifies the wrapped token as canonical and mints additional wrapped tokens on chain B. This inflates the total wrapped supply beyond the backing reserve. The underlying issue is an incomplete or mutable token address registry that does not enforce a strict canonical-to-wrapped mapping, combined with absent supply reconciliation between the source and destination bridge contracts. Any minting on the destination side must be conditional on verified, finalized, and un-replayable lock events on the source side for verified canonical tokens only.
affected_patterns: bridge failing to distinguish between native token deposits and wrapped token deposits
missing token registry mapping canonical token addresses to their wrapped counterparts across chains
bridge accepting wrapped token deposits and minting additional wrapped tokens on destination chain
no supply reconciliation mechanism between source and destination bridge contracts
token address mapping in bridge registry updatable by a single admin without governance vote or timelock

entries.title: Bridge Liquidity Pool Drain via Fraudulent Withdrawal Proofs
entries.description: Optimistic bridges and ZK bridges where withdrawal proofs can be forged, or where the fraud challenge period is insufficiently short, allow attackers to drain the bridge liquidity pool. In optimistic designs, the attacker submits a fraudulent state root claiming a large deposit, waits out a challenge period that is too short for honest parties to detect and respond, then withdraws funds. In ZK designs, the risk is a subtle edge case in the proof verifier circuit that causes the verifier to accept an invalid proof (as occurred in the Wormhole Solana verification bug). Critical mitigations: enforce a minimum 7-day challenge period for optimistic bridges, implement an accessible and incentivized fraud proof submission mechanism, subject ZK verifier contracts to formal verification, disallow withdrawals during active challenge periods, require withdrawal proofs to be cryptographically linked to specific deposit transaction hashes, and impose withdrawal rate limits on liquidity pools.
affected_patterns: optimistic bridge challenge period configured under 7 days
no fraud proof submission mechanism or interactive challenge game for disputed state roots
ZK proof verifier contract accepting invalid proofs due to arithmetic edge cases or missing range checks
bridge allowing withdrawals to proceed during an active, unresolved challenge period
withdrawal proof not cryptographically linked to a specific deposit transaction on the source chain
bridge liquidity pool lacking withdrawal rate limiting or per-block withdrawal caps

entries.title: Cross-Chain Replay Attack on Bridge Transactions
entries.description: Bridge transactions lacking chain-specific identifiers or unique per-channel nonces can be replayed on different chains or different bridge deployments. An attacker intercepts a legitimate bridge message (e.g., a signed deposit proof), replays it on a different target chain or a different bridge instance on the same target chain, and double-claims tokens. This is analogous to the EIP-155 replay protection problem on standard Ethereum transactions. Each bridge message must embed both a source chain ID and a destination chain ID (using block.chainid or a hardcoded chain-specific domain separator), and nonces must be scoped per source-destination pair — not global — to prevent cross-channel nonce reuse. Messages from chains sharing the same chain ID (test networks, forked chains) require additional domain separation.
affected_patterns: bridge message missing source chain identifier in its signed payload
bridge message missing destination chain identifier — message valid on any chain
bridge nonce not scoped per source-destination chain pair, allowing nonce reuse across channels
bridge contract using block.chainid without EIP-155-style replay protection domain separator
same bridge contract deployed with identical addresses on multiple chains sharing the same nonce space

entries.title: Bridge Exit Mechanism Denial of Service
entries.description: Bridges where the exit (withdrawal) mechanism can be congested, blocked, or griefed allow attackers to trap user funds indefinitely. Attack vectors include: flooding the exit queue with dust withdrawals to exhaust available processing capacity; submitting withdrawals whose proof verification is so gas-intensive that the transaction cannot fit within the block gas limit; bribing or controlling the sole relayer or sequencer to censor specific withdrawal transactions; and depleting exit liquidity tokens to make the exit path economically infeasible. Emergency exit mechanisms (e.g., forced inclusion via L1 calldata, direct state proof submission) are essential safety valves. Without them, a DoS on the normal exit path permanently locks funds. Bridges should cap the exit queue depth, cap proof verification gas, mandate decentralized relay networks with censorship resistance, and provide a permissionless emergency exit path.
affected_patterns: bridge exit queue unbounded with no maximum pending withdrawal limit
withdrawal proof verification gas cost exceeds block gas limit for large or adversarial proof batches
single relayer or sequencer with no permissionless forced-inclusion fallback
bridge exit requiring a specific token that can be made artificially scarce by an adversary
no emergency exit mechanism allowing users to bypass the normal queue via L1 direct submission

entries.title: Chainlink L2 Sequencer Downtime Stale Price Consumption
entries.category: L2 Sequencer and Oracle Failure Modes
entries.description: On L2 networks (Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, and similar rollups), when the sequencer goes offline, Chainlink decentralized price feeds stop receiving updates because no transactions can be included. However, the feeds' latestRoundData() function continues to return the last known price with an outdated timestamp. Lending protocols and derivatives platforms that consume these feeds without checking the L2 Sequencer Uptime Feed (a Chainlink-provided contract that signals whether the sequencer is live) will treat stale prices as current. This allows users to borrow against artificially inflated collateral (using pre-crash prices during sequencer downtime), avoid liquidations, or execute arbitrage against the stale price. Additionally, a grace period must be enforced after sequencer restart — prices immediately post-restart may still lag real market conditions. Protocols must: (1) check the L2 Sequencer Uptime Feed, (2) confirm the sequencer has been live for at least a grace period (e.g., 60 seconds), and (3) validate price timestamp freshness relative to the sequencer's last restart time.
affected_patterns: L2 protocol calling Chainlink latestRoundData() without first checking the L2 Sequencer Uptime Feed contract
missing grace period enforcement after sequencer restart before trusting newly updated prices
protocol not comparing price feed answer timestamp against the sequencer's last-confirmed restart timestamp
latestRoundData() result used directly without staleness timestamp validation on L2 deployment
hardcoded heartbeat staleness timeout that does not account for variable sequencer downtime durations

entries.title: Sequencer Transaction Ordering Manipulation (L2 MEV)
entries.category: L2 Sequencer and Oracle Failure Modes
entries.description: L2 sequencers hold complete authority over transaction ordering within a block — a power far exceeding what any single miner/validator holds on L1 due to the sequencer's monopolistic position. A malicious or compromised sequencer can front-run profitable transactions (e.g., large DEX trades), back-run liquidations, or censor specific addresses indefinitely. This Sequencer Extractable Value (SEV) is structurally different from L1 MEV because there is no competitive mempool to provide ordering transparency or competing relayers to enforce fairness. Protocols with time-sensitive operations — auctions, liquidations, TWAP updates — must account for sequencer ordering risk. Mitigations include: verifying the existence of a forced inclusion mechanism (transactions submitted directly to L1 that the sequencer must eventually include), avoiding reliance on block.timestamp provided by the sequencer for security-critical logic, and providing L1-based emergency paths for time-critical operations.
affected_patterns: protocol assuming fair ordering on L2 with no forced transaction inclusion mechanism
time-sensitive operations (liquidations, auctions, TWAP snapshots) with no L1 fallback path
security-critical logic relying on block.timestamp set exclusively by the sequencer without bounds checking
no mechanism for users or protocols to bypass the sequencer for emergency transactions
smart contract using randomness derived from sequencer-controlled block variables

entries.title: L2 State Root Submission Delay and Pre-Finalization Exploitation
entries.category: L2 Sequencer and Oracle Failure Modes
entries.description: Optimistic rollups post state roots to L1 with a time delay (typically 7 days) during which any party can submit a fraud proof to invalidate an incorrect root. Protocols that treat L2 transaction execution as final before the L1 state root is confirmed and the challenge period has passed are exposed to state reversion attacks. If the L2 state is later invalidated, transactions that appeared fully confirmed are rolled back, potentially causing double-spending or leaving counterparties with invalid accounting. This is particularly dangerous for cross-chain protocols that credit funds or release collateral on L2 state before L1 finalization. Protocols must clearly distinguish between L2 execution (soft finality) and L1-confirmed finalization (hard finality) and apply appropriate delays to any operation that cannot be reversed.
affected_patterns: bridge accepting L2 state as final before the L1 challenge period has fully elapsed
cross-chain message relay relying on an unfinalized L2 state root not yet confirmed on L1
protocol crediting user funds based on an L2 transaction receipt before state root finalization
no reorg or state reversion protection for time-sensitive L2 operations involving external value
L2-to-L1 message processed and funds released before the dispute/challenge period concludes

entries.title: Oracle Price Feed Aggregator Multi-Source Failure and Stale Round Detection
entries.category: L2 Sequencer and Oracle Failure Modes
entries.description: Chainlink and similar aggregator-based oracle systems can enter states where the returned data is invalid or stale. This occurs when: multiple data sources simultaneously go offline causing the aggregator to lose quorum; a round fails to complete (answeredInRound < roundId signals an in-progress or failed round); or the aggregator returns a zero price. Protocols that do not validate these conditions treat invalid oracle data as legitimate market prices, enabling borrowing against zero-value collateral, skipping liquidations, or triggering erroneous liquidations. The complete validation checklist for latestRoundData() is: (1) revert if price <= 0, (2) revert if answeredInRound < roundId (stale/failed round), (3) revert if updatedAt timestamp exceeds the maximum acceptable staleness threshold, (4) implement a circuit breaker that pauses the protocol if the oracle has been stale beyond a configurable maximum. A fallback oracle (e.g., Uniswap TWAP) should activate automatically when the primary aggregator fails.
affected_patterns: protocol not checking answeredInRound == roundId from Chainlink latestRoundData() before using price
protocol accepting price == 0 from oracle aggregator without reverting or falling back
no circuit breaker or pause mechanism when oracle returns data stale beyond acceptable threshold
missing fallback oracle activation when primary Chainlink aggregator loses quorum or goes offline
protocol using a single oracle source with no redundancy or cross-validation against secondary source

entries.title: L2 Gas Price Oracle Manipulation via L1 Base Fee Distortion
entries.category: L2 Sequencer and Oracle Failure Modes
entries.description: L2 networks calculate transaction fees by querying an on-chain L1 gas price oracle that estimates the cost of posting transaction data to Ethereum as calldata. If this oracle uses the spot L1 base fee (rather than a time-weighted average), an attacker who can influence L1 base fee (e.g., by flooding the L1 mempool) can temporarily spike L2 transaction costs to uneconomical levels, pricing out legitimate users or frontrunning operations that rely on gas estimates. Conversely, suppressing L1 base fee can make L2 transactions artificially cheap, enabling spam or DoS attacks. The L1 gas oracle itself, if updatable by a single address without governance, is also a direct manipulation target. Protocols must use smoothed or capped gas price inputs, apply min/max bounds to fee calculations, and require multi-sig or governance-timelocked oracle updates.
affected_patterns: L2 gas oracle reading spot L1 base fee rather than an exponential moving average or smoothed value
gas price oracle contract updatable by a single EOA address without governance or timelock
protocol hardcoding L2 gas estimates for operations instead of dynamically querying the gas oracle
no gas price ceiling or floor in L2 fee calculations allowing extreme fee values to pass through
L1 base fee manipulation (via mempool flooding) directly propagating into L2 transaction cost predictions

entries.title: Flash Loan Governance Vote Manipulation
entries.description: An attacker borrows a large quantity of governance tokens via flash loan within a single transaction, uses that temporary voting power to create or vote on a governance proposal, then repays the loan — all in one atomic block. This is possible when the governance system records voting power at the time of the vote rather than at the time of proposal creation (or at a prior block snapshot). The Beanstalk protocol attack ($182M, April 2022) demonstrated this precisely: the attacker used a flash loan to acquire a super-majority, passed an emergency governance proposal that sent the entire treasury to the attacker's wallet, and repaid the loan in the same transaction. Robust governance must use snapshot-based voting (ERC-20Votes / ERC-20VotesComp checkpoint model), enforce a minimum token holding period before votes become eligible, and reject delegations that take effect within the same block as the vote.
affected_patterns: governance snapshot recorded at vote-casting time rather than at proposal creation block
no minimum token holding period before tokens are eligible for voting or delegation
governance contract accepting freshly delegated votes within the same block as the delegation transaction
governance token lacking snapshot-based checkpoint voting (ERC-20Votes) — uses live balance instead
proposal creation and proposal voting executable within the same transaction or block without delay

entries.title: Governance Token Concentration and Whale Vote Dominance
entries.description: When a small number of addresses or coordinated entities hold majority voting power in a governance token distribution, the protocol's governance is effectively centralized despite its on-chain form. A single whale or a colluding group can pass any proposal — treasury drains, fee parameter changes to benefit themselves, or upgrades to inject malicious code — without the broader community being able to resist. This is exacerbated by low quorum thresholds that can be met by a single large holder, and by treasury withdrawal proposals that require only a simple majority of a low quorum. Mitigations include: quadratic voting, vote delegation caps, minimum quorum thresholds set as a percentage of circulating (not total) supply, time-weighted voting power, and multisig-based treasury access requiring broader consensus.
affected_patterns: single address holding more than 10% of total governance token supply with no voting power cap
top 5 addresses collectively controlling more than 50% of total voting power
quorum threshold set below the practical participation rate — achievable by a single large holder
treasury withdrawal proposal executable with fewer than 5% of total supply participating in vote
no per-address voting power cap or quadratic voting mechanism to limit whale dominance

entries.title: Delegation Sandwich Attack and Vote Weight Override
entries.description: In governance systems with on-chain token delegation, an attacker can execute a delegation sandwich: delegate voting power to themselves just before a voting snapshot block, cast votes, then immediately undelegate — net cost is only transaction fees. More severe variants include chaining delegations across multiple controlled addresses to amplify apparent voting weight (though checkpoint-based systems prevent double-counting, poorly audited implementations may not). Delegation to address(0) permanently destroys voting power as a griefing vector against governance participation. Governance systems must enforce a cooldown period between delegation changes, prevent circular delegation loops, revert on delegation to address(0) if the intent is to preserve voting power, and use per-block checkpoint accounting (ERC-20Votes) that prevents mid-block delegation abuse.
affected_patterns: delegation changes taking effect immediately in the same block without a lockup or cooldown delay
no cooldown period between successive delegation changes allowing rapid delegate-vote-undelegate cycling
delegation mechanism allowing circular delegation loops that could cause accounting inconsistencies
delegation to address(0) silently accepted, effectively burning votes as a governance griefing attack
checkpoint-based voting system not correctly accounting for mid-block delegation changes

entries.title: Timelock Parameter Bypass and Governance Delay Manipulation
entries.description: Governance timelocks are the primary defense against malicious proposals — they enforce a mandatory delay between approval and execution, giving the community time to detect and react. Attackers targeting the timelock itself can neutralize this protection: (1) pass a proposal to reduce the timelock delay to zero or near-zero, then immediately execute a treasury drain in a second proposal; (2) add themselves as a new proposer/executor role on the timelock; (3) use a batch proposal to combine a timelock parameter change with a malicious action, executing both simultaneously. The Tornado Cash governance attack (2023) used a malicious proposal with a hidden self-destruct-and-redeploy trick to gain permanent control of the governance contract. Mitigations: enforce an immutable minimum timelock floor, require higher quorum for proposals that modify timelock parameters, restrict delegatecall in timelock executors, and validate proposal payload hashes at submission to prevent substitution.
affected_patterns: timelock delay modifiable by governance with no hardcoded minimum floor (e.g., can be set to 0)
timelock admin/proposer role transferable within the same proposal as a malicious treasury action
batch proposal execution that combines a timelock delay reduction with a treasury drain in one transaction
governance timelock executing delegatecall to an arbitrary user-supplied target address
proposal description hash not validated at execution — allows payload substitution after approval

entries.title: Proposal Griefing and Governance Denial of Service
entries.description: Governance systems can be rendered non-functional by adversarial participants who exploit the governance mechanics to prevent legitimate proposals from passing or reaching execution. Attack vectors include: creating an unlimited number of spam proposals (if no minimum token balance is required), exploiting a proposal cap to block the queue and prevent urgent security fixes from being submitted, systematically voting against every proposal to consume quorum and block progress, and inflating the governance token holder count via dust attacks to push the effective quorum requirement beyond what honest participants can meet. Critical security fixes require a fast-track emergency governance path (ideally a guardian multisig with limited emergency powers and a short-duration window) to ensure that protocol-breaking vulnerabilities can be patched without waiting for a full governance vote cycle.
affected_patterns: no minimum governance token balance requirement for proposal creation, enabling spam proposals
proposal submission limit per time period absent or set high enough to enable queue flooding
quorum calculated from total token supply including locked, burned, or permanently inactive tokens
no emergency governance bypass mechanism for critical security vulnerability patches
vote-against griefing carries no token cost or reputational penalty to the griefing actor

entries.title: Governor Contract Upgrade Hijacking via Self-Governance
entries.description: When the governance contract itself is upgradeable and the upgrade authority is controlled by the governance contract (i.e., the governor is its own admin), an attacker who accumulates sufficient voting power can submit and pass a proposal that upgrades the governor to a malicious implementation. The malicious implementation may remove timelocks, disable quorum requirements, grant permanent admin access to the attacker, or simply drain all protocol treasury in the same transaction. This represents the ultimate governance attack because it permanently and irreversibly undermines every other safety mechanism in the system. Mitigations: the governor contract's upgrade authority should be held by an independent multisig (not the governor itself), the upgrade proxy admin should be explicitly excluded from governor control, upgrade proposals should require a supermajority quorum significantly higher than normal proposals, and an immutable guardian address should retain veto power over self-upgrades.
affected_patterns: governor contract is upgradeable and the upgrade is controlled by the governor itself (self-admin)
no external guardian multisig or independent body with veto power over governor upgrade proposals
governor upgrade proposal requiring no higher quorum than standard parameter-change proposals
governance contract proxy admin address set to the governance contract itself — circular control
no immutable safety rails or hardcoded invariants preventing governor self-upgrade to a malicious implementation

entries.title: Governance Oracle and External Data Dependency Manipulation
entries.description: Governance proposals that condition their execution on external on-chain data — oracle prices, token balances on other chains verified via bridge messages, or off-chain vote tallies submitted by a single relayer — introduce an attack surface where the governing condition can be manipulated independently from the governance process. An attacker can corrupt the external data source to make a proposal execute under false pretenses. For example: a proposal that triggers a collateral parameter change when an oracle price is above a threshold — the attacker manipulates the oracle to satisfy the condition at execution time. Mitigations: validate oracle prices within governance execution with tight bounds checks, use multi-source data with anomaly detection, require cross-chain vote data from at least one independent verifier, and apply a mandatory delay between data observation and proposal execution to reduce flash manipulation risk.
affected_patterns: governance proposal reading and acting on oracle price at execution time without bounds validation
cross-chain governance relying on a single unverified bridge message for vote tally import
proposal execution conditional on external contract state manipulable by a third party
off-chain vote result submitted by a single trusted relayer without cryptographic multi-party verification
governance proposal using block.timestamp for time-gated execution without sequencer-proof verification on L2

entries.title: Vote Buying, Dark DAO Collusion, and Governance Bribery
entries.description: Vote buying in on-chain governance occurs when a third-party contract or off-chain coordination mechanism compensates token holders for voting in a specific direction, enabling a minority of capital to capture governance outcomes by purchasing votes from passive or economically motivated holders. Dark DAOs are trustless vote-buying platforms implemented as smart contracts: token holders deposit their governance tokens into the Dark DAO, which programmatically casts votes in the direction chosen by whoever paid the highest fee, then distributes proceeds to depositors. Because the entire process is on-chain and non-custodial, it is difficult to prohibit. More subtle forms include governance bribery protocols (e.g., Votium, Hidden Hand) that explicitly offer compensation for votes. Defenses include: vote privacy via commit-reveal schemes, time-weighted lock requirements that raise the cost of vote aggregation, and constitutional governance rules that make purchased-vote outcomes legally and technically challengeable.
affected_patterns: governance token wrappable into a third-party contract that controls vote delegation on behalf of depositors
no vote privacy mechanism — all votes publicly visible on-chain allowing buyer verification and payment
token holders able to trustlessly commit their future vote direction to a third-party smart contract
delegation to a contract address that programmatically casts votes based on highest-bidder instructions
governance reward or bribe distribution mechanism tied to specific voting direction rather than participation

entries.title: Permit2 Universal Allowance Widening and Cross-Protocol Drainage
entries.description: Uniswap's Permit2 contract centralizes token approvals: users grant Permit2 a maximum allowance, then use off-chain signatures to authorize individual protocol operations. An attacker who obtains a user's Permit2 signature (via phishing, malicious DApp, or front-running) can use it to transfer tokens across any protocol integrated with Permit2, not just the intended one. The risk is amplified when: (1) the allowance amount is set to type(uint160).max without an expiration, (2) the signed spender field is the Permit2 contract itself rather than a specific target contract, or (3) the DApp requests a batch approval covering multiple tokens beyond what the operation requires. Permit2 signatures are off-chain, leave no visible on-chain approval record, and are difficult for users to audit or revoke without specialized tooling. Protocols integrating Permit2 must request the minimum necessary amount with short-duration deadlines and restrict spender to the specific contract address.
affected_patterns: Permit2 approval signature authorizing type(uint160).max token amount without expiration deadline
Permit2 signature not scoping the spender field to a specific protocol contract address
user signing a Permit2 batch approval covering multiple tokens without clear per-token scope explanation
protocol requesting Permit2 approval with a broader token amount or longer duration than the specific operation requires
Permit2 approval with no deadline or a deadline set far in the future (e.g., year 2106)

entries.title: EIP-2612 Permit Signature Frontrunning and Griefing
entries.description: EIP-2612 permit() allows token approvals via off-chain signatures submitted as transaction parameters. When a user submits a permit() + transferFrom() as separate transactions (or as individual calls in a multi-step flow), an attacker monitoring the public mempool can front-run the permit() call with an identical signature — setting the allowance to their preferred amount or address before the user's transaction executes. The user's transaction then either reverts (if the nonce is already consumed) or is a no-op. A more severe variant: the attacker sandwiches the permit by calling permit() to set the allowance, then immediately calling transferFrom() to drain the approved tokens before the user's intended operation executes.
