Smart contracts that integrate permit() must use try/catch around the permit call (and proceed if the allowance is already set), submit permit+transferFrom atomically in a single transaction, or use private mempools (e.g., Flashbots Protect) to prevent frontrunning.
affected_patterns: permit() call submitted as a separate transaction from the subsequent transferFrom(), creating a frontrun window
smart contract calling permit() and reverting on failure instead of checking if allowance is already sufficient
permit transaction broadcast to the public mempool without private submission or bundled execution
contract not using try/catch around permit() call — single-point griefing possible by frontrunning the permit
no check for existing allowance before calling permit(), making the flow brittle to permit replay

entries.title: ERC-721/ERC-1155 NFT Permit Nonce Reset on Transfer (EIP-4494)
entries.description: NFT permit standards (EIP-4494 for ERC-721, various ERC-1155 extensions) face a unique replay vulnerability when nonces are scoped to the token ID rather than to the owner's address. If a user signs a permit for tokenId 42, transfers the NFT to another address, and later receives the same tokenId 42 back (e.g., via a marketplace purchase or transfer), the previously-signed permit may become valid again if the token's nonce was not incremented during the transfer. An attacker who retained the original permit signature can submit it against the returned NFT to gain an unexpected approval. Correct implementations must either: (1) tie nonces to the owner address (not the tokenId), (2) increment the tokenId nonce on every transfer (not just on permit use), or (3) invalidate all outstanding permits when a token changes ownership.
affected_patterns: ERC-721 permit nonce scoped to tokenId rather than to the owner address
permit signature remaining valid after the NFT is transferred to a new owner and returned
missing permit nonce increment or invalidation when the NFT token changes ownership via transfer
ERC-1155 permit implementation lacking an operator-scoped nonce tied to the specific owner address
permit deadline set to type(uint256).max, creating an effectively permanent approval for NFT spending

entries.title: Permit Signature Phishing via Malicious DApp or Fake UI
entries.description: Unlike approve() transactions (which appear visibly on-chain and require gas), permit() and Permit2 signatures are off-chain operations with no gas cost — users are less suspicious of signing requests. Attackers deploy phishing websites or malicious DApps that request permit signatures from users under false pretenses (e.g., 'sign to verify your wallet' or 'sign to claim your airdrop'). The signed permit is then submitted by the attacker to drain the user's tokens. Because the permit is executed by the attacker's transaction, the user's wallet history shows no approval and the drainage is often attributed to an unknown transfer. This attack vector was responsible for hundreds of millions in losses during 2023-2024 NFT and DeFi phishing campaigns. Mitigations (for protocol developers): request permits only for amounts strictly necessary for the immediate operation, use very short expiration deadlines (minutes, not days), and clearly display human-readable permit data in the signing request UI.
affected_patterns: DApp requesting permit approval for token amounts significantly exceeding the specific transaction's need
permit signature request covering tokens not involved in or relevant to the stated DApp operation
off-chain permit signature request presented without a clear human-readable breakdown of amount and spender
permit approval request for contract addresses not matching the DApp's verified and audited contracts
Permit2 batch signature request covering multiple unrelated tokens in a single phishing-optimized request

entries.title: Permit2 Batch Transfer Atomicity Failure and Partial Approval Exploitation
entries.description: Permit2 batch operations (permitBatch and transferFromBatch) allow multiple token approvals or transfers to be processed in a single call. If individual transfers within the batch can fail independently without reverting the entire batch, the operation leaves the contract in an inconsistent state: some allowances are set, some are not; some transfers executed, others did not. An approved-but-not-transferred allowance can be exploited by the approved spender in a separate transaction after the partial execution. Furthermore, protocols that mix ERC-20 and ERC-721 transfers in the same batch may face asymmetric failure modes — ERC-721 transfers revert on missing approvals while ERC-20 transfers silently return false (in non-reverting implementations). Batch operations must be fully atomic: any individual transfer failure must revert the entire batch and all associated allowance changes.
affected_patterns: Permit2 batch approval operation without guaranteed atomicity — partial success leaves inconsistent approval state
batch transfer not reverting on individual transfer failure, leaving remaining allowances unexpectedly active
allowances set for the entire batch upfront before transfers execute, with no rollback on partial failure
no rollback mechanism for partially-executed batch approvals leaving stale allowances exploitable
batch operation mixing ERC-20 and ERC-721 token transfers with different revert/return-false failure modes
